title: Defensive Resources
subtitle: Only moves, counter-blows, and saving the game with checks.
goals: Find the single move that survives
Answer a threat with a bigger threat
Rescue lost positions with perpetual check

steps.say: Every lesson so far has been about attacking. This one is about the other half of chess — the half that decides most games between club players. Three defensive skills: finding the ONLY move, meeting a threat with a bigger one, and — when the position is truly lost — forcing a draw by perpetual check. White is a whole rook down here. Watch what he can still do.

steps.prompt: You're a rook down and losing. Save the half-point — start the perpetual!
hints: You cannot win. You can, however, check forever — if every check leaves the king exactly one square.
Qe8+ forces Kh7 (the only legal move), and Qh5+ forces the king straight back to g8. Repetition = draw.

line.say: Check along the back rank — and the king has exactly ONE legal answer...
...and now the h-file check forces him straight back. One legal move again.

The position has repeated. Black is a rook up and cannot escape the checks: if he ever blocks, he loses the blocking piece; if he runs, there is nowhere to run. Draw by repetition — half a point rescued from a lost game.

rejections.say: A quiet approach move: Black answers ...Rb1+ and mates or queens. In a lost position the ONLY plan is a forced series of checks — Qe8+ starts it.
You centralize instead of checking — and ...Rb1+ follows, converting the extra rook at leisure. Only forcing checks matter here.

steps.wrongSay: Lost positions are saved by checks, not by good moves. Which check leaves the king one square?
steps.successSay: Perpetual check: the swindler's parachute. Before you resign, always count your checks.

steps.prompt: You're Black, facing a back-rank threat with your king boxed in. Defend — permanently.
hints: Rd8+ is coming, and you have nothing on the back rank to stop it. Make a door for the king instead.
h6 (or g6) gives the king air. One pawn move and the back rank threat is gone forever.

line.say: Luft. Now Rd8+ is met by Kh7 and White has achieved nothing. The cheapest defensive move in chess: spend one tempo, delete an entire family of threats.
Air on the other flank — the back rank is no longer a mating square, and the king can breathe on g7.

rejections.say: It opens f7 for the king, but weakens e6 and the a2–g8 diagonal permanently — and after Rd8+ Kf7 the king is out in the open. The safest luft comes from the ROOK pawn: h6.

steps.wrongSay: The threat is mate on the back rank. Give your king a square before it becomes urgent.
steps.successSay: Prophylactic defence: fix the weakness before the attack arrives, not during it.

steps.prompt: Black's queen has invaded on d5, eyeing your loose pieces. Don't cower — challenge her!
hints: Retreating or bracing leaves her dominating the board. Can you challenge the invader directly?
Qxd5 offers the trade on your terms — an invader is only strong while she is allowed to stay.

line.say: The simplest defence in chess: trade off the attacker. An invading queen with no partners is just a piece — and once she is gone, every threat she carried disappears with her.

rejections.say: A defensive pawn move that weakens the king's diagonal and does nothing about the queen. When defending, prefer moves that CHALLENGE the attacker over moves that merely brace for it.
It guards nothing that matters and creates a new hole on c3. Passive defence loses slowly; active defence — trade or challenge — ends the problem.

steps.wrongSay: You have two active answers: trade her off, or hit her with a rook. Pick one.
steps.successSay: Trade, challenge, or counterattack — three active defences, all better than shuffling.
